title: The Twofold Knowledge and the Eye of the Heart
english: The light of God is perceived at once, providing sight and enlightening it. To those who are blind and do not know Him when He rises, He grants even more: to have the eyes of the mind and to perceive the light. In this way, the covenant is not suddenly released; rather, if someone today makes himself worthy to be the son of the One who possesses and is an heir, then it is revealed to him. 'My eyes are continually toward the Lord' (Ps 25:15). Since 'the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous' (Ps 34:15), it is necessary that the righteous also have their eyes continually toward Him.

They do not see Him at all times, but sometimes [they see] one of the forbidden things; for just as 'no one can serve two masters' (Matt 6:24), so no one can have his eyes toward God and toward evil or the maker of evil first. God is a spiritual essence seen by the eyes of the intellect. When the eyes of the intellect are stretched toward Him alone, they see nothing else. And the physical hands are not able to see when we see God, just as one serving God is not able to serve Mammon.

And regarding 'is not able' I say this: he is not able to do justice while he is doing injustice; for I do not say as I say 'it is not possible for a man to fly,' but rather that as far as he is righteous, he is not able toward sin, and when he is a sinner, he is not able toward virtue. 'My eyes' therefore 'are continually toward the Lord' (Ps 25:15). I always see Him. And he who sees God does not sin; 'everyone who sins has not seen Him nor known Him' (1 John 3:6). And behold the piety of the saints; even if he himself chooses to direct his eyes toward the Lord, it is evident that he is not sinning; the achievement of sinlessness is inscribed by God: 'since my eyes are continually toward Him' (Ps 25:15), because of this I escape the snare which sin prepares; for 'He Himself will rescue my feet from the snare' (Ps 124:7).

I searched for some of the ancients, which is a fine thing to say, that sometimes the eye is named in the singular of the inner man, and sometimes in the plural. In the Song of Songs, for instance, it is said: 'You have made us one from your eyes' (Song 6:9). 'My eye brought forth tears.' 'My eye was troubled from my spirit.' But in the plural: 'I lifted up my eyes to the mountains' (Song 6:4); and in the present verse: 'my eyes...'

Because of all things toward the Lord. And 'having been enlightened the eyes of the heart' (Eph 1:18). We have a twofold knowledge; for then it is knowledge of truth, when the form of each thing being known is received into itself.

The works of God are both visible and invisible; and from the greatness of these and from their beauty, the one who constructed them is perceived. And our mind is an eye seeing the invisible, the pure heart, which also sees God. And we also have the sense of eyes. And if it applies to the visible works of God in this way, as they were constructed and possess nature, it is healthy. But when, I say, seeing the sun we think it is God himself, seeing the heavenly arrangement we regard as mere idle chatter, this eye does not see correctly; for it was necessary 'that the invisible things of God be seen through the works of the creation of the world' (Rom 1:20).

The invisible things of God are seen then, when we apply [our sight] to the visible creations of God and thus from the creation of this sensible world we see clearly the invisible things of God. We are not able to see the arts and the sciences in the minds of men except when the mind is invisible. And from the constructed works or scientific contemplations we receive the sense of the mind, according to what science or art has made it. Primarily, therefore, one perceives the science of the mechanic; he who is able to receive the principles of mechanical constructions into his own intellect. Similarly also regarding others; we call that one a physician who knows medical matters as they ought to be, as the science dictates.

When, therefore, someone sees the invisible as it ought to be—and by 'as it ought to be' I say, as it is possible—and sees also the invisible creations of God, of which the human soul is also [a creation], he has this eye seeing toward God and pure through all things. When he also correctly perceives the sensible creations and the providence concerning them, he has the sensory desire—not this I mean the one of the body, but the intellect of the sensibles, the visible—succeeding, and thus he has the eyes toward the Lord through all things.

As a slave speaks. And a slave is the one serving God, who both in disposition and in deed confesses the lordship, 'he who does the will of the Father in the heavens' (Matt 7:21). 'Because he himself will drag the feet out of the snare' (Ps 91:3).
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Uniqueness of the Only-Begotten Son
english: Even if the trappers and hunters seek to catch my foot, as if to throw it into a trap, I do not suffer this because I keep my eyes toward the Lord at all times. For often the settings of the wicked snares are called the disciplines of the Divine: 'the foot was caught in that trap which they hid' (Ps 7:15). Frequently the enemies of truth prepare traps, and by catching others in these traps, they themselves are snared. And there is such a thing in history: Haman prepared wood in order to crucify the righteous Mordecai, and he himself was crucified upon it. And concerning this great man it is said: 'He dug a pit and hollowed it out, and he will fall into the pit which he made' (Prov 26:27). Even if these things do not happen in this life, they certainly happen in the life to come, caught in the trap which he prepared.

For many observe these sensory things and consider themselves to be escaping them, such as: 'all who take a sword will perish by the sword' (Matt 26:51). But this is not a contradiction; rather it says: those who take a sword will fall under punishment. In many places of the Scriptures the sword signifies punishment, as in: 'I will drink my arrows, and my sword devours the blood of the wounded' (Ps 11:6), and: 'my sword was drunken in heaven' (Ps 73:4); for it also touched those who sinned in Psalm 86 and drew them toward punishment in this way: 'our soul was snatched like a sparrow from the trap of the hunters' (Ps 86:7). And see the difference: perhaps some of those being hunted by these wicked hunters are taken entirely into the traps, while others only their feet. Therefore those saying: 'our soul was snatched like a sparrow' were caught entirely. You say immediately: 'the trap was broken, and we were snatched away.'

Here, since the saint has his eyes toward the Lord at all times, concerning more trivial sins he says: 'my feet became a trap.' Therefore, snap them out of there, so that having become otherwise unfooted, they may run the way of the commandments of God and say: 'I ran without iniquity and I directed my course' (Ps 119:45). 16 Watch over me and have mercy on me. When God watches, mercy comes to those being watched; for they are worthy of being seen; for the [one who...]

By sinning, one is distanced from the eyes of God and from His face. Adam, indeed, when he sinned along with Eve, 'was hidden from the face of the Lord God' (Gen 3:8). They do not endure being seen by the face of God when they most clearly realize to themselves that they have sinned. But Cain, acting impudently, led himself away from the face of God; for 'Cain went out.' And the one going out does so by choice. Concerning Adam and Eve, it is said: 'the Lord cast them out.' While they were still inside, He cast them out; for it was no longer permitted for them to be inside. Nevertheless, they were surrounded by desire. They are not as evil as the one who went out from the face of the Lord. These are those about whom it is written: 'lawless ones do not abide before your eyes' (Ps 119:19). But they go outside the eyes of God voluntarily; for the eyes of God, beholding, enlighten those who are looked upon. 'For I am poor and only-begotten' (Ps 31:6).

Aetius, the leader of the Eunomian heresy, says to some: 'How great a thing you grant by saying that the Christ is the only-begotten of God. And many other creatures are only-begotten. The sun, indeed, is only-begotten.' I say to him: it is not the same thing to be something 'only-begotten' and to be an only-begotten offspring or an only-begotten Son. Therefore, these things said to others as 'only-begotten' are not said with the addition of 'Son,' or 'from the Father,' or 'offspring.' But the Savior, if He is ever so named, is called with such an addition: 'and we beheld His glory, a glory as of the only-begotten from the Father' (John 1:14). And the one who is the only-begotten Son from the Father is the Father's only. And again: 'so God loved the world that He gave His only-begotten Son' (John 3:16). I say: since there is an only-begotten Son, it is impossible for there to be another son belonging to that only-begotten Son. And nothing of the creatures is only-begotten; for even if the sun were only-begotten, it is not an only-begotten creature, nor an only-begotten work, but an only-begotten sun. So also among humans we say 'only-begotten child,' not because he is the only one that exists, but because he is the only one to that parent. And that: 'he who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God' (John 3:18). Since, therefore, he who says these things is not an only-begotten Son, let us observe how he is called otherwise; for even if [he speaks of] David the...

title: The Meaning of Only-Begotten and Tribulation
english: If you take a man, he was not an only-begotten. He had six other brothers. Therefore, it must be avoided to say 'only-begotten' in this way, as in: 'And I myself was left alone, and they seek my soul to take it' (Ps 142:4). By what logic they say the sun is only-begotten, by the fact that there is no other sun; so when the saint is made solitary and separated from other men by life and contemplation, he is only-begotten. 'Only-begotten' therefore means 'I am and [I am] poor.'

Yet he who is thus poor is rich; for he 'is rich' in every sense and in all knowledge. But toward the God who looks upon him and bestows gifts, he is poor; just as Abraham said: 'Since I have begun to speak to the Lord, I am indeed dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27)—for he did not say 'dust and ashes' all at once, but 'since I have begun to speak to the Lord'—so also Moses, though trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and possessing sufficiency regarding speech, called himself 'heavy-tongued and slow of speech' (Ex 4:10) from the time he began to speak to your servant. And this man, therefore, even if he is rich—for nothing is richer than he who has his eyes always toward the Lord—yet toward the one looking upon him and showing mercy, he saw himself as poor.

And it is also possible to say 'only-begotten' meaning 'I have only one soul.' This being caught, it escapes from the snare; for to me it is only-begotten. The tribulations of my heart have widened. Not in every case, I say, do tribulations widen, but for the one bearing them bravely. The apostle writes this: 'In all things being afflicted, but not in anguish' (2 Cor 4:8).

Those knowing the Hebrew dialect say that to be in anguish, when it is named after tribulation, signifies the intention of being afflicted, the being in anguish from not bravely bearing the afflictions, such as Job, who 'in all things being afflicted was not in anguish' (Job 1:21); for how could he be in anguish, he who says: 'As it pleased the Lord, so it happened; let the name of the Lord be blessed'? And the apostles coming out from the council, because they were dishonored for the name (Acts 5:41), were not being afflicted according to the disposition, but were rejoicing. And regarding sensible things, the one contending for the crown of expectation, seeing it lying before his eyes, bravely bears the wounds, and rejoices that, being struck, he does not falter.
